strengths: The proposed EMAG mechanism is simple, training-free, and architecture-agnostic (attention-space EMA), making it easy to adopt and to compose with existing guidance techniques (CFG, APG, CADS, ERG, S2), which the paper demonstrates concretely in Tables 1/3 and the supplementary material.

Broad and fairly systematic experimental coverage: class-conditional (DiT-XL/2 at 256² and 512²) and text-conditional (SD3-Medium/MMDiT) settings, conditional and unconditional generation, multiple metrics (FID, Precision/Recall/Density/Coverage, CLIPScore, HPS), and numerous ablations (layer choice, EMA scale, guidance scale, halflife/beta) reported both in the main paper and an extensive appendix.

The paper is transparent about baseline adaptation choices (how SAG/SEG/PAG/ERG/S2/APG/CADS were ported from U-Net to DiT/MMDiT backbones), which aids reproducibility and fair comparison, and includes full hyperparameter tables (Table S11) and prompts used for qualitative figures (Table S12).

The Hopfield-network perspective (Sec. 3.4.3, Appendix A) offers a plausible, if informal, interpretive lens for why attention-space EMA yields “hard” yet faithful negatives, complementing the empirical study with some conceptual grounding.

Consistent, non-trivial HPS improvements over CFG and other tested guidance baselines across most experimental settings, together with qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 4, S7-S11) illustrating subtle artifact correction rather than gross distortion.
weaknesses: FID and diversity metrics are frequently worse for EMAG than for competing baselines (e.g., Table 3: CADS FID 18.32 vs. EMAG 22.98/EMAG+CADS 19.95; Table S8: EMAG FID 4.16 vs. CFG 2.30, S2 2.40, CADS 2.70; Table S9: EMAG FID 7.59 vs. CFG 3.08; Table S9 unconditional-style recall for EMAG is drastically lower, e.g., 0.094 vs. 0.532 for CFG), indicating a real precision/diversity trade-off that is not fully reconciled with the paper's framing around “preserving core structure” and complementing autoguidance-style diversity goals.

The central quantitative claim rests heavily on HPS, a learned human-preference proxy known to be susceptible to reward-hacking / aesthetic over-optimization; the paper offers no human study or cross-validation with other preference/quality proxies (e.g., ImageReward, PickScore) to confirm that HPS gains reflect genuine perceptual improvement rather than metric-specific bias, which is a notable evidentiary gap given CFG's documented over-saturation tendencies that HPS-like metrics can reward.

The adaptive layer-selection strategy, one of the paper's stated contributions, does not clearly outperform simple fixed-layer choices in the reported ablation (Table 4/S7: fixed layer L8 attains better FID and HPS than the "Adaptive" variant on SD3), so the practical benefit of the proposed statistics-based selection over a manually tuned fixed layer is not convincingly established.

The theoretical (Hopfield) motivation is explicitly described as an "interpretive analogy" without a rigorous derivation connecting the EMA update to provable energy-descent or quality guarantees in the diffusion setting; the paper defers formal treatment to future work, weakening the claimed theoretical grounding.

No analysis of computational/memory overhead from maintaining per-layer EMA state across timesteps, nor runtime comparisons against baseline guidance methods, leaving practical deployment cost unclear.

Scope is limited to two Transformer-based image backbones (DiT, SD3/MMDiT); generalization to U-Net-based diffusion models, other modalities, or larger/varied text-to-image benchmarks is not empirically tested, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which tempers the claimed generality of the approach.

Some presentation issues remain, including a seemingly counter-intuitive statement about EMA halflife and perturbation strength (Sec. 3.4.1) that is not clearly justified, and generally dense notation/equations that could be streamlined for clarity.

strengths: Proposes a conceptually clean, training-free mechanism (EMA over self-attention maps) to construct a controllable 'weak' model for auto-guidance-style negative signals, unifying and extending prior attention-perturbation guidance methods (SAG, SEG, ERG, PAG) under one framework.

Introduces a statistics-based adaptive layer-selection rule (MAE between attention and its EMA) that removes the need to hand-pick a fixed layer, and ablations (Table 4/S7) show this adaptive rule balances the FID/HPS trade-off better than any single fixed layer or applying the perturbation to all layers.

Broad and reasonably rigorous experimental protocol: two different transformer backbones (DiT-XL/2 and MMDiT/SD3), both class-conditional and text-conditional settings, multiple resolutions (256²/512²), and consistent evaluation code/data/sampling steps across all baselines, which supports fair comparison.

Demonstrates plug-and-play compatibility with orthogonal SOTA guidance techniques (APG, CADS, S²), showing additive HPS gains when combined, which is a practically useful property for a guidance module.

Extensive and transparent supplementary material: hyperparameter sweeps for every baseline, per-task hyperparameter tables, additional qualitative figures, and an interesting (if informal) Hopfield-network-based motivation for why EMA-smoothed attention induces convergent, semantically-faithful negatives.
Qualitative comparisons (Fig. 2/3, supplementary S8-S12) visibly show EMAG producing subtler, more structure-preserving degradations than S², SAG, SEG, ERG, supporting the 'hard negative' narrative.
weaknesses: FID results are frequently worse than several baselines (e.g., Table 3: EMAG FID 22.98 vs. SAG 18.74, CADS 18.32, APG 21.82; Table S8: EMAG FID 4.16 vs. CFG 2.30, CADS 2.70, S² 2.40), so the central claim of 'competitive' fidelity is only partly supported and the paper leans heavily on HPS gains that could partly reflect a bias of HPS toward sharper/more saturated images rather than genuine fidelity improvement.

All quality claims rely exclusively on automated proxies (HPS, FID, PRDC, CLIPScore); despite the paper's emphasis on 'semantically plausible' and human-preference-aligned outputs, no human study or additional preference metric (e.g., PickScore, ImageReward, user study) is provided to corroborate the HPS-based narrative.

The theoretical Hopfield-network connection (Sec. 3.4.3, App. A) is offered mainly as a qualitative/interpretive analogy rather than a predictive theory; the authors themselves acknowledge the fixed-point/one-step-retrieval theorems do not strictly apply to the continuous, entangled diffusion attention setting, limiting its explanatory value beyond intuition.

The method requires a fairly large number of task/architecture-specific hyperparameters (β half-life, τs/τe, δ, layer range, EMAG scale w_e; see Table S11), each separately tuned per backbone/resolution/task, which raises practical reproducibility and generalization concerns despite the detailed reporting.

Some reported differences between configurations are small (e.g., EMAG-I 29.56 vs. EMAG 29.68 HPS) without variance estimates or repeated-seed statistics, making it hard to judge the reliability/significance of the reported improvements.

Scope is limited to image generation with two transformer backbones; extension to video/audio/3D is left entirely to future work (reasonable but reduces the immediate breadth of impact claimed in the introduction).

strengths: The paper proposes a clear, well-motivated training-free guidance mechanism (EMAG) that generates 'hard negatives' via exponential moving averages of self-attention maps, with an interpretable knob (decay factor β) controlling degradation strength, and an adaptive per-timestep layer-selection rule based on MAE statistics — a meaningful refinement over prior fixed-layer perturbation schemes (SAG/SEG/PAG/ERG).

Extensive and systematic experimentation across two backbones (DiT-XL/2 class-conditional and SD3-Medium text-to-image), at multiple resolutions, in both conditional and unconditional settings, with Pareto-frontier analyses (FID/HPS/Precision/Recall), multi-seed variance estimates, hyperparameter sweeps for all baselines, and reduced-step-budget robustness checks.
Good coverage of complementary/orthogonal guidance combinations (APG, CADS, S², ERG), demonstrating EMAG composes with these methods and typically improves HPS further.

Recognizes and addresses its own main practical limitation (computational overhead of maintaining EMA over post-softmax attention) by introducing EMAG-Q, with a reasonable first-order Taylor-expansion argument for why query-space EMA approximates attention-space EMA, and empirical validation (CLIP-I/DINO similarity, SRCC/PLCC) that the approximation holds.

Thorough and transparent appendix documentation of baseline adaptation choices, architectural incompatibilities (e.g., PAG with MMDiT joint attention), and honest discussion of limitations/ethical considerations.

The negative-sample 'hardness via cosine similarity' analysis (Fig. 2) and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 4) provide reasonably convincing, if indirect, evidence for the core claim that EMAG produces more fine-grained/semantically faithful negatives than coarser perturbation baselines.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative improvement is modest: the reported HPS gain of +0.54 over CFG is small in absolute terms, and in several tables (e.g., Table 2) EMAG does not improve, or slightly worsens, FID relative to CFG or other baselines (e.g., CADS achieves much lower FID); the paper leans heavily on HPS as the primary evidence of benefit, which is a single learned preference-proxy metric and could reflect biases of that specific model rather than a universally verifiable quality improvement (no human user study is conducted).

Standard EMAG incurs substantial computational overhead (+213% runtime, ~1.7x peak memory in Table 4) relative to CFG; while EMAG-Q reduces this to +95%, this is still far more expensive than the baselines it aims to outperform, and the trade-off in practical deployment terms is not strongly justified by the size of the quality gains.

The Hopfield-network theoretical section (Appendix C) is presented as an 'interpretive analogy' rather than a rigorous derivation specific to the proposed method; it recycles existing convergence theorems from Ramsauer et al. without deriving new guarantees for EMAG itself, and its explanatory value is largely qualitative/post-hoc rather than predictive.

The method involves a fairly large number of interacting hyperparameters (β, λ, τs, τe, δl, layer range, EMA scale w_e, CFG scale) whose settings differ across tasks/backbones (Table S12), which raises reproducibility and practical-adoption concerns despite the extensive ablations provided.

Baseline methods originally designed for U-Net architectures are re-implemented/adapted by the authors for DiT/MMDiT backbones (with some acknowledged architectural incompatibilities, e.g., PAG), which, despite being transparently documented, introduces potential risk of implementation bias favoring the proposed method in the comparisons.

The adaptive layer-selection mechanism is a greedy heuristic (largest MAE) without a more principled optimization criterion; the authors themselves note this as an avenue deferred to future work, suggesting the current selection strategy, while empirically helpful (Table 5), is not fully justified theoretically.
